title: Renunciation
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: Shuko Edie Norton takes up renunciation, a word Shuko has puzzled over since Reb Anderson's retreat in the 1990s, and works through it using Norman Fischer's Sailing Home, Suzuki Roshi, and the Latin root of the word. Shuko sets it beside Fra Angelico's Annunciation in Florence and Shuko's own joy at learning of being pregnant. Shuko concludes that renunciation means giving up the belief in a separate self, and tells of a second cat who learns to beat the first into her lap each morning, as a picture of catching the mind quickly. Shuko returns to zazen mind and to Dogen's phrase "letting go of self-centered life," found in arriving on time, entering the zendo quietly, and volunteering for a job.

sentences.text: In my earlier Way Seeking Mind talk, I spoke about what I've observed my mind doing as I've been struggling with my relationship with my adult sons, which has turned out to be, at least currently, different from what I had expected.

Today I want to continue to give some observations about my mind and how it works, and the struggles I've had around an idea that has been interesting to me for a long time: renunciation as an important aspect of Zen practice.
I puzzled over that for a while, and I thought back last fall, when I learned I was to give a dharma talk, why don't I take that on, because I don't know what it really means.
So it's kind of like cooking a dinner you've never made for your guests before, taking that chance.
I'm taking the chance here, and I hope it'll turn out all right.
Whereas I have no intention of renouncing my sons, there are elements in my thinking about them and my relationship with them that I am working on relinquishing, a form of renunciation.
But first I want to give a disclaimer.

I'm going to describe how my mind has been working with this concept the past few weeks, and what I'm going to say is what I thought so far, certainly not the first or last word on this pretty complex topic.
Your mind, if you're lucky, doesn't work like mine does, but I hope that you will find something in this talk that's useful to you, if nothing else as a cautionary tale.
What may come to mind when we think about renunciation is the monk entering the monastery and leaving the world behind, relinquishing the world.
This has long been a Christian tradition, and as we know, it's possible to do this in Zen as well.
A Zen student can go to a number of monasteries in the US and in Europe and Asia and stay for a duration, maybe years.

When I lived in Japan, I entered and stayed for several weeks in a Zen training temple for Europeans and Americans in Okayama, Japan, and there I had the interesting experience of having no contact with the rest of the world, Japanese or American.
I actually didn't like that.
I was glad to get out and start reading the newspaper again.
How do we relate to the practice of renunciation if we're doing non-monastic lay practice, living our daily lives in the world as we are doing?
Do we have to renounce anything, and what to renounce if we do?
The concept of Buddhist renunciation first came to my attention back in the 1990s at a retreat led by Reb Anderson.
My initial reaction to the topic was "Whoa, I don't like the sound of that."
I started resisting the idea that I might have to give up something even before I heard what it was.
As he explained, renunciation was not about rejecting or giving up anything.
It was more about meeting whatever comes with no requirements.
It is about renouncing our preferences and desires for things to be the way we want them to be.
It is about not asking reality to be anything other.
Or as Norman says in his beautiful book Sailing Home, which I read again this past couple of weeks, and I'm quoting here:
*The present moment is essentially and always a moment of renunciation.
Renunciation is simply cooperation with the way things are.
Moments do pass away.
Resisting this natural unfolding doesn't change it.
Resistance only makes it painful.*
Or as Suzuki Roshi put it, renunciation is not about giving up the things of the world but accepting that they go away.
Renunciation is just letting things be what they are, regardless of what we'd prefer.
These definitions make sense to me.
However, for some reason I have found them really hard to hold on to in my mind in the midst of my daily life.
Over and over again, when confronted with an unexpected or unwanted change, I find my mind takes over and I react defensively, resisting and complaining about the new reality.
Sometimes I realize quite soon that I'm resisting, but sometimes I'm way down the road of resistance and well into the pain before I realize what's happening, that I have grabbed hold once again.
Why this habit of resistance is so hard to catch early, let alone to avoid altogether, is a significant question for me.
So I've been interested in exploring the idea of renunciation more deeply for this talk.
Start again with a simple statement: to avoid or end our suffering, we must stop, renounce, desiring things to be other than what they are.
Okay, I get that for a few seconds, but then I lose it again.
Partly the reason renunciation seems elusive to me is that often it's defined by a negative: not adding anything to something, not clinging, not wanting something to be other.
It's hard for me to hold on in my mind a negative action, so the idea and requirements of renunciation remain fuzzy.
Logically, renunciation derives from the Latin *renunciare*, which means to proclaim or protest against.
*Nutare* means to announce, and *re* in this case is "against," not "again" as in redo or return or rejoin.
So: announce against something, presumably something that's already been announced or proclaimed or agreed to.
It's kind of public in that way.
Musing further about the word renounce, I think of its linguistic opposite, which means to say something aloud to someone else.

Last fall I was in Italy, and in Florence I visited the San Marco Museum, the church where Fra Angelico has many beautiful frescoes, among them the Annunciation, in which the Archangel Gabriel is depicted announcing to Mary that she is to bear a child.
This painting is at the top of two long stairways, two broad long stairs, so you just kind of emerge into it when you go up these stairs.
In this painting both Gabriel and Mary look very tender, humble, in awe of each other, in awe of the moment.
Given that Mary, as we're told, was a virgin and the child was to be the Christ, one can understand the feeling the painting conveys.
Fra Angelico was depicting perhaps the great announcement of Western civilization, at least up until that time.
Seeing this painting made me recall the time when I felt something of the same awe and tenderness that Fra Angelico depicts.
This was when I realized that I was pregnant with my second child.
It was a moment of great joy and light, as if an angel had visited me.
A few years earlier, at age 22, I found out I was pregnant with my first child.
I was excited but also quite anxious about what I was going to undergo in this experience.
But this second time, having known the joy of having my first child, I was really deeply happy to realize I would have another one.
So for me personally, the idea of enunciation conveys the feeling of great beauty and joy.
Reflecting on the momentousness of enunciation causes me to wonder if renunciation also carries some greatness, a great rejection or a great repudiation.
Plus there's certainly something of the element of a public statement in both enunciation and renunciation: announcing to the world the Christ, denouncing to the world.
What the public aspect seems to imply is that renunciation is a big act, a major act, in my mind.

Now, we know in Buddhism that in order to end our suffering we are advised to renounce our desires and preferences, and this is a difficult thing to do, given how quick our preferences are to claim dominion over us.
But I'm wondering if there isn't something even deeper that renunciation is aimed at.
I'm thinking that if renunciation is a big, a major act, the thing being denounced must itself be big, otherwise it wouldn't require a big action to reject it.
So what is so important and so resistant to rejection that we have to denounce it, claim it invalid, untrue, that it doesn't even exist?
Isn't it our idea that we have a self, our assumption that we have and are a permanently abiding, unique individual self, separate and distinct from everything and everyone else?
That old Buddhist bugaboo, that self, may be so strongly entrenched in us that it requires the power of renunciation to dislodge it.
So my thinking has gone.
Now, thinking that we have a separate self is natural for us.
It's how our minds work, our conditioned minds.
Our minds are educated, conditioned from childhood to believe we are and have an inviolable individual self, and it's always been and always will be here.
At least in the Western world this is the case, not so much in Japan, where group is seen as more important than the individual.

But here it's hard for us not to believe we have a self, even when we learn through Buddhism that the reason we feel alienated and alone, and thus unhappy, comes from our belief that we are separate from everyone else.
Yet despite our unhappiness, our conditioned minds seem to do anything and everything to perpetuate this illusion of ourself.
In fact, Rodney Smith claims that our sense of self doesn't care if we're happy or not.
It just wants to be perpetuated.
According to Smith, it is the conditioned mind that perpetuates this illusion.
Moreover, the self is actually only a formation of the mind, like the Heart Sutra says about the emptiness of all forms: sensations, perceptions, formations, consciousness are also like this, empty.

The ordinary thinking mind, the one that observes and analyzes and judges and plans and does a myriad of other useful functions and is essential to our survival, but there are some things it just can't do, such as understand that its creature, the self, is an illusion.
We know how strong and powerful our minds can be.
If the idea of the self is the primary battleground of the mind, one can see that we might have to have a powerful action to fight our mind and break down this illusion.
We may need to denounce the idea of ourself.

We may need to proclaim to ourself and others that ourself doesn't exist permanently and separately, that in fact we exist only in and through relationship with everything and everyone else, co-arising moment by moment and therefore insubstantial in any ongoing way.

So underneath the kind teachings I mentioned earlier, the advice to us to cooperate with the way things are, to renounce wanting reality to be other than what it is, to give up wanting to have more choices than our lot in our lives and reality actually is offering us, underneath these sensible and gentle recommendations we can see that in order to give up our preferences, we actually have to give up believing we have a self, a separate enduring self, and give up clinging to it.

Now, doing that might take a lot of energy, to give up our lifelong assumption that we are a self, that we are an entity that requires perpetuating and defending, that we feel like we are the center of the universe.
That takes a big powerful expression, an announcement against the basic tenet of Western thought that there is me and there is you and we're not connected.
A bold renunciation indeed.

So to answer my earlier question about lay practice, do we have to renounce and if so what, we can answer yes: we must renounce the illusion that we have a permanently abiding nature or self, despite all the evidence our conditioned minds immediately and continually provide us in nearly every instance of our daily life to keep us thinking that we are separate and unique selves.
We actually are empty, which is the condition called anatta.
Now be aware that renunciation of the concept of self actually contradicts the entire trajectory and momentum of Western civilization and the English language, both of which are grounded in dualism.
No wonder we're confused: sinner and savior, right and wrong, good and evil, inner and outer, self and other, et cetera, et cetera.
To counter this vast and powerful army of dualistic assumptions that we have, we, as members of Western civilization, may need the power and energy of announcing against, of renunciation.
In our cultural tradition, renouncing the self, claiming it doesn't exist, is indeed a great announcement of renunciation.

So far in this talk I have been demonstrating how my mind has been grappling with this idea, my eager, energetic, problem-seeking and problem-solving mind that loves to pounce on a concept and batter it into submission.

Given how strong-headed my mind seems to be, it looks like I need to power up in order to face down my mind's illusion of self, or maybe I need to become more alert, quicker on the draw, when my self defenses leap up.
A quick story may illustrate.
I once had a kitten, an Angora kitten, who grew into a beautiful Angora cat, whom I felt eventually was lonely at home without me while I was at work.
So I ended up adopting another cat to be her companion.
However, as you might guess, the new cat immediately disliked the original cat.
The original cat was fine with it; the new cat hated the original cat.
Especially she didn't like the fact that as soon as I sat down in the morning for breakfast, the original Angora cat jumped up into my lap and was happy.
The new cat sat on the floor, growled and glared at the original cat every morning for the first week she was there.
But the next Monday morning, as soon as I sat down at the table, the new cat beat the original cat into my lap.
She had learned to be quick if she wanted to have the prize spot.
So maybe, like that second cat, I need to be quicker to beat my mind to the punch when I see my selfish defenses taking over.
Now, I'm a pretty intuitive person.
I assess and respond to my experience and other people kind of from my gut, from the awareness that I've developed over the years in zazen.

But I hadn't realized until recently how quickly my mind takes over, intercepting my intuitive, heartfelt response to an event or person and applying the mind's analytical problem-solving skills, running over and casting aside my natural heart-centered response.
Some years ago, when I was more in the world of work and confounded daily by other people's behavior, I think I may have stayed longer with my intuition.
But in the past few years, being retired and not mixing so much, my thinking mind has gained a strong foothold.

Realizing this recently, I've begun to practice with greater attention to these moments when myself starts to jump up and take over and claim authority, and I'm beginning to find a simpler, more direct way to work with my overactive mind.

It is to practice staying with my body and breath, remaining quiet and in the present, holding at bay my mind with its insistence on defining or explaining what is happening, allowing myself to be aware of only the present moment, not letting my mind take over with its preferences for things to be different from what they are.
This simpler, quieter way is, of course, zazen mind, or one aspect of it: the awareness that allows us to apprehend what is actually happening without distorting it with our desires and preferences.

As Norman has put it in Sailing Home, and I paraphrase here, the practice of just living and accepting what is, moment to moment, allows us to come home to where we started and where we have always longed to be, to our true present experience.
So all the puzzlement and consternation and drama of figuring out what renunciation is and isn't is just my conditioned mind working, doing what it knows how to do.

The act of renunciation instead is simply accepting reality as reality, what is given, and working with that, only that, and as things change, accepting that they are changing and cannot do otherwise, and then working.

So although renunciation of the self has powerful results, I'm thinking that the act of renouncing the self can be gentle and natural, arising, as it must, not from the mind but from the body and the heart that are just cooperating with the way things are.

So as lay practitioners, non-monastic practitioners, householders with jobs and families, each of which arenas can tend to reinforce the illusion that we have and are a separate self that we must defend and perpetuate, as lay practitioners we have the opportunity of returning again and again to our cushion in the zendo and in our home practices, and mentally, as we endeavor to practice zazen mind in our daily lives.
Of course, as we know, that practice can be a big challenge.

But once we have, and then have again and again, the experience that zazen gives us of quieting down and allowing our awareness to expand, we can rely on zazen mind to help us let go of our egoic, defensive, conceptually oriented self.
Better yet, through our practice in sangha together we have the perfect opportunity to experience renunciation as Dogen defined it: the opportunity to let go of self-centered life.

So if it's hard to remember, as it has been for me, that renunciation means letting go of our preferences and not expecting more of reality than what it offers, it may be easier to remember that when we practice together we actually do let go of our self-centered life.
When we sit quietly in the zendo, when we enter or leave the zendo or change positions in zazen quietly so as not to disturb others, we are letting go of self-centered life.
When we arrive on time for zazen, when we volunteer for a job at the zendo, when we show up as we promised we would to fill an essential role at a retreat, we are letting go of self-centered life.

When something needs cleaning or fixing or improving at the center and we just do it, we are letting go of our illusion of—when sitting in zazen with our eyes softly open so that our awareness broadens beyond our own mental activity, and we have that aha moment in which we realize, wow, everyone else in this room is suffering too, we are letting go of self-centered life.
And when we realize that our zazen encourages everyone else's zazen, as well as benefiting everyone in the world, we are letting go of self-centered life.
In order to practice together in sangha, we must let go of our self-centered life.
Definition: when we focus on what will be best for everyone, that is a sangha.
We relinquish ourself naturally.
We see what is real, we do what is needed, we don't worry about it, and our self just melts away.
